meta.title: Who really said "Our greatest glory is not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Confucius. This maxim was written by Oliver Goldsmith in The Citizen of the World (1762) and only reassigned to Confucius by 1831.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Our greatest glory is not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Confucius. Oliver Goldsmith wrote it in The Citizen of the World (1762); it was reassigned to Confucius by 1831.

answer.label: Not Confucius — actually Oliver Goldsmith
answer.sourceLine: The line was written by the Anglo-Irish author Oliver Goldsmith in “The Citizen of the World” (1762), where it is spoken by his fictional Chinese philosopher Lien Chi Altangi: “Our greatest glory is, not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.” Because the character was a Chinese sage, readers assumed the wisdom was genuinely Chinese, and by 1831 it had been re-labelled “Confucius.” No text in Confucius’s own writings contains it.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

source.excerpt: We should feel sorrow, but not sink under its oppression … Our greatest glory is, not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.
trail: Oliver Goldsmith, “The Citizen of the World” (1762), Letter VII — the primary text literally reads “Our greatest glory is, not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall” (Internet Archive full text).
Quote Investigator finds no evidence Confucius wrote it and credits Goldsmith; it notes the maxim was reassigned to Confucius in The Royal Lady’s Magazine by 1831.
Wikiquote lists the line under Goldsmith, sourced to The Citizen of the World, not among Confucius’s genuine sayings.
source.excerptNote: Goldsmith gave a second version in Letter XXII: “True magnanimity consists not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.”

source.rightsNote: Goldsmith’s “The Citizen of the World” was first published in 1762 and the author died in 1774, so the work and this sentence are firmly in the public domain worldwide.

author.name: Oliver Goldsmith
author.heading: The real author
author.bio: Oliver Goldsmith was an Anglo-Irish writer of the London literary circle around Samuel Johnson, celebrated for the novel The Vicar of Wakefield, the comedy She Stoops to Conquer and the poem The Deserted Village. In 1760–61 he published a series of satirical letters in The Public Ledger, written in the voice of an imaginary Chinese visitor to London; collected in 1762 as The Citizen of the World, they are the true home of this ‘Confucius’ maxim. He died in London in 1774.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone says ‘Confucius’
misattribution.intro: The wording is genuine 18th-century English prose — but it was never Confucius’s. It only sounds Chinese because Goldsmith deliberately put it in the mouth of a fictional Chinese sage.

items.why: No line matching this appears in the Analects or any authentic Confucian text. Quote Investigator shows the credit to Confucius first appears around 1831, in The Royal Lady’s Magazine — roughly 70 years after Goldsmith wrote it.
An 1900 anthology, Gems of Literature, reassigned the saying to Emerson; there is no basis for this in his works, per QI.
Both are recorded using the adage in the 20th century (Lombardi via Bart Starr in 1969; Mandela at a 1998 White House reception), which spread it further — but neither originated it, as QI documents.

misattribution.truthLine: The true author is Oliver Goldsmith, who wrote it in The Citizen of the World (1762).

context.heading: A quote designed to be mistaken
lead: Goldsmith’s book is a satire: an imaginary Chinese philosopher, Lien Chi Altangi, writes home to describe the absurdities of London life. To make the device convincing, Goldsmith seasoned the letters with grave, aphoristic ‘Eastern’ wisdom — including this line about falling and rising.

The disguise worked too well. Readers took the maxims for real Chinese proverbs, and over the next century editors quietly swapped the fictional Lien Chi for the most famous real Chinese sage they knew: Confucius. It is a misattribution the author practically engineered.
context.pull: The line only sounds like Confucius because Goldsmith built it to.
